chunks: From him, from Ibrahim ibn Abi Bakr ibn Abi Sammak, from Dawud ibn Farqad, from Abdul A'ala, the slave of the progeny of Saam, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I said to him, 'Say: O Allah, Master of the Kingdom, You give the kingdom to whom You will and take away the kingdom from whom You will.' Is it not that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, gave the kingdom to the Banu Umayya?' He (peace be upon him) said, 'It is not as you think. Indeed, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, gave us the kingdom, and the Banu Umayya took it, like the man who has a garment and another takes it; so it does not belong to the one who took it.'

key_terms.الثَّوْبُ: The garment/clothing (used as an analogy for possession)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between the kingdom given to the Imams and the kingdom of the Umayyads according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (as) distinguishes between divine sovereignty (mulk) granted to the Ahl al-Bayt and the transient political rule (mulka) seized by the Umayyads, employing the analogy of a garment to illustrate that mere possession does not confer rightful ownership. This hadith, found in al-Kafi, underscores the Shia theological concept that true authority remains with the Imams despite their political absence, while usurpers hold power only by divine permission and temporary decree. The explanation clarifies that the verse 'He gives sovereignty to whom He wills' applies to both, but the quality and legitimacy of that sovereignty differ fundamentally.
